items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to conduct one-tailed hypothesis tests in cases where the null hypothesis can be modeled using a Poisson distribution.

Content:
Suppose an online shop typically receives [MATH: 25] orders per day. The owner suspects the average number of orders has dropped after poor online reviews. They decide to conduct a hypothesis test at the [MATH: 5\%] significance level to determine whether their suspicions are correct.

Content:
Let [MATH: \lambda] be the average rate number of orders received per day. Then, we have the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Content:
- [MATH: H_0: \:\:\lambda = 25]
- [MATH: H_1: \:\:\lambda < 25]

Content:
The significance level is [MATH: \alpha = 5\%.] Furthermore, we'll assume that events occur independently and at a constant average rate. Therefore, if the null hypothesis is true, we have
[MATH: X \sim \textrm{Po}(25).]

Content:
Suppose the shop received [MATH: 15] orders on a randomly selected day after the reviews were posted. Does this data provide enough evidence to reject [MATH: H_0?]

Content:
Using a CDF table for the Poisson distribution, the value of our test statistic is

Content:
[MATH: P(X ≤ 15)|= 0.0223 = 2.23% < 5%.]

Content:
Let's interpret this result:

Content:
- Since [MATH: P(X \leq 15) < 5\%,] the experimental result is unlikely under the null hypothesis.
- In other words, there is sufficient evidence to reject [MATH: H_0.]
- Therefore, we conclude that the order rate has reduced.

sections.normalized_html:
A hypothesis is a statement about a population parameter that we wish to test by collecting sample data.

In this case, the population parameter we wish to test is [MATH: \lambda,] the average number of bicycles rented daily.

  • The default assumption is that the average number of bicycles rented is the same as before. Therefore, the null hypothesis is [MATH: H_0: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lambda = 13}.]

  • The manager wishes to test the hypothesis that the average number of bicycles rented per day has increased. Therefore, the alternative hypothesis is [MATH: H_1: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lambda > 13}.]

  • Under the null hypothesis, the rentals occur independently at a constant average rate of [MATH: 13] per day. Therefore, [MATH: X\sim \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{Po}(13)}.]

  • The manager conducted an experiment and found that [MATH: 19] bicycles were rented on a particular day. Therefore, a suitable test statistic is [MATH: P(\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}X\geq 19}).] Note that:

    • Since we wish to test [MATH: \lambda > 13,] this is a right-tailed test.

    • We're interested in [MATH: X\geq 19,] not just [MATH: X=19.] This is because we also want to include all events in the right tail that more unlikely than [MATH: X=19.]
